So I've been learning about and building a compiler for the MeTTa programming language. And I realised something:

Lean could be the most performant language in the world, and it could also be the future.

Let me explain, so in a normal compiler, an optimisation is only possible when static analysis can conservatively establish that the transformation is safe.

If it can’t prove it cheaply, the compiler has to preserve the general case.

And in JIT, there is runtime trace based optimisations where the jit analyses hot loops and optimises for them on the spot. It specializes around that trace and inserts guards so it can deoptimize if its assumptions turn out to be wrong. And there is CPU branch prediction, which saves our cpus like 99% of the actual execution or whatever.

Point is what does this all mean. well, lean has the advantage that not only it is a programming langauge, but writing code, is writing math, which means that:

The compiler, and the runtime, can skip out on substantially a lot more work, because it can mathematically gaurantee bounds, making it much more performant.

Now already Modern compilers already solve a huge amount of low-level optimization extremely well: register allocation, instruction selection, vectorization, inlining, loop optimization, constant propagation, etc.

Now having lean's mathematical gaurantee's on top of that, and you have the most performant programming langauge in the world.

because with Lean, you can have actual proofs:

  • this index is always in bounds
  • this branch is impossible
  • these two regions can never alias
  • this value is always positive
  • this loop executes exactly N times
  • this state can never occur
  • this function is equivalent to another function
  • this data structure always satisfies some invariant

It is well known that the largest optimisation that you can do in systems level programming is moving things that are runtime computed to compile time computed.

and the other unnecessary states can literally be removed from the program.

And the effect compounds.

Prove one branch impossible -> remove it.

That makes a value statically known -> specialize a function.

That specialization makes an allocation unnecessary -> remove it.

That proves aliasing impossible -> reorder/vectorize operations.

That creates dead code -> remove it.

Eventually the IR handed to the ordinary backend could be dramatically smaller and simpler than the program the developer originally wrote.

Then LLVM/Clang/etc. can do what they already do extremely well on that reduced program.

the main idea is that it could mean less runtime work, fewer checks, fewer branches, fewer allocations, smaller reachable state spaces, more specialization, and potentially much smaller/simpler code reaching the machine-code backend.

I would say people are generally aware of this fact and using it already, for example Std.TreeMap knows to eliminate some branches in its modification logic due to its invariants, people regularly used verified indices etc.

@Henrik Böving Nice to hear, I wonder if it would be the next rust. That would sound very appealing to me, not only that, but with the rise of LLM generated code, this would also provide strong feedback to LLMs and help them write better code.

I don't think that with a reference counted language you will be able to match Rust in general but we might end up getting quite good in some areas and of course writing DSLs etc. in Lean is also a possiblity
